title: Confirming Customer Details
subtitle: How to ask for, repeat, and confirm a customer's name, email, and phone number
description: Every customer relationship starts with getting the details right. This lesson teaches the simple, professional language you need to ask for a name, email address, and phone number — and how to read them back to make sure everything is correct before you save it.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley sets up Marcus's account and confirms all his contact details

vocabulary.definition: Information about a person or order — for example, their name, email address, and phone number. In sales, you always confirm the details before you create an account.
vocabulary.example: Riley said: Before I set up your account, I need to confirm a few details. Could you give me your full name, email, and phone number?

vocabulary.definition: To say or write the letters of a word one by one. You ask a customer to spell their name when you want to write it correctly.
vocabulary.example: Marcus said his last name was Oliveira. Riley said: Could you spell that for me? Marcus said: O-L-I-V-E-I-R-A.

vocabulary.definition: Right and without any mistakes. After you repeat the details back, you ask: Is that correct?
vocabulary.example: Riley read the email back to Marcus and asked: Is that correct? Marcus checked and said: Yes, that is correct — you have it right.

vocabulary.definition: To say something again. You ask a customer to repeat a detail when you did not hear it clearly or want to double-check.
vocabulary.example: Riley did not hear the phone number clearly. She said: Could you repeat that for me? I want to make sure I have the right number.

vocabulary.definition: Officially recorded in a system. A registered email is the one linked to a customer's account — it is the one they use to log in.
vocabulary.example: Riley asked: Is this your registered email? Marcus said: Yes — that is the one I use for everything. My login and my invoices all go there.

vocabulary.definition: To change information in a system to make it correct and current. When a customer gives you new details, you update their profile.
vocabulary.example: Marcus gave Riley his new phone number. Riley said: Thank you — I will update that in our system right now. You will see the change in your account.

vocabulary.definition: Information used to reach someone — such as their email address or phone number. In B2B sales, you always collect contact details for every new customer.
vocabulary.example: Riley said: I need your contact details before I can create the account. Can I get your email and phone number?

vocabulary.definition: To check something a second time to make sure it is right. It is always good to double-check details before saving them.
vocabulary.example: Riley finished writing the email address and said: Let me double-check that — marcus.oliveira@techcorp.com. Is that right?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: Could you spell that for me?
phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask this when you need to write a name, email, or word correctly — letter by letter. It is professional and shows you care about accuracy.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus gave his last name. Riley said: Could you spell that for me? I want to make sure I write every letter correctly in the system.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: Let me read that back to you
phrasalVerbs.definition: Use this before you ask 'Is that correct?' You repeat the details out loud so the customer can hear them and catch any mistakes.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley said: Let me read that back to you — marcus.oliveira@techcorp.com, plus 44 7911 123456. Is everything correct?

phrasalVerbs.definition: A simple, direct question to confirm that the information you have is right. Always ask this after you read the details back.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley repeated the email address and asked: Is that correct? Marcus listened and said: Yes, that is correct. You have it exactly right.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: What is the best email to reach you?
phrasalVerbs.definition: A professional way to ask for an email address. 'Best email' shows you understand the customer may have more than one.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley asked: What is the best email to reach you? Marcus said: Use my work email — marcus.oliveira@techcorp.com. That is the one I check every day.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: Could I take your phone number?
phrasalVerbs.definition: A polite, standard way to ask for a phone number. 'Could I take' is softer than 'Give me' and sounds more professional.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley had the name and email. She said: Could I take your phone number as well? I want to have a way to call you if there is ever an issue.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: I will update that in our system
phrasalVerbs.definition: Say this after the customer confirms their details. It tells them you have saved the information and everything is official.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus confirmed everything was correct. Riley said: Perfect — I will update that in our system now. You will receive a confirmation email within a few minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Marcus, before I set up your account, I need to confirm a few [[details:information about a person — like name, email, and phone number]]. Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Of course. Go ahead.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Could I take your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: It is Marcus Oliveira.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Could you [[spell:to say the letters of a word one by one]] that for me? The last name.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Sure — O-L-I-V-E-I-R-A.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Got it, thank you. And what is the best email to reach you?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: It is marcus.oliveira@techcorp.com.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Let me read that back to you — marcus.oliveira@techcorp.com. Is that [[correct:right and without any mistakes]]?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Yes, that is correct.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Perfect. And could I take your phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Yes — it is plus 44 7911 123456.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Let me [[double-check:to check something a second time to make sure it is right]] — plus 44 7911 123456. Is that right?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Yes, perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Great. I will [[update:to change information in a system to make it correct]] that in our system now. You are all set, Marcus.

completeSentenceExercise.instructions: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence. Only one answer is correct.

items.sentence: Could you _____ your last name for me?
items.explanation: 'Spell' means to give each letter one by one — exactly what you need to write a name correctly. 'Say' just means to speak. 'Write' is something the customer cannot do for you over the phone.

items.sentence: Let me read that _____ to you — is everything correct?
items.explanation: 'Read that back' is the fixed phrase — it means repeating information you just received so the other person can confirm it. 'Again' and 'over' do not work in this phrase.

items.sentence: Is this your _____ email — the one linked to your account?
items.explanation: 'Registered' means officially recorded in the system. It is the specific word for the email connected to an account. 'Main' and 'work' are too informal for this context.

items.sentence: I will _____ that in our system right now.
items.explanation: 'Update' is the correct professional word for adding or changing information in a system. 'Refresh' means reloading a page. 'Change' is too general.

items.sentence: Could you _____ your phone number? I did not hear it clearly.
items.explanation: 'Repeat' means to say something again so you can check it. It is the most natural and professional word here. 'Say' and 'give' do not imply you want to confirm — just hear it once.

items.sentence: Before I set up your account, I need to confirm a few _____.
items.explanation: 'Details' is the correct word for specific information like name, email, and phone number. 'Facts' is for general information. 'Things' is too informal for a professional conversation.

chooseResponse.instructions: Read what the customer says. Choose the best response from the three options.

options: Could you spell that for me? I want to write every letter correctly.
items.explanation: Option A is the right move — an unusual or unfamiliar name should always be spelled out to avoid mistakes. Option B assumes you heard it correctly without checking. Option C is irrelevant at this point.

options: Let me read that back to you — thomas.johansson@globalcorp.com. Is that correct?
Could I take your phone number?
items.explanation: Option B is correct — always read the email back to confirm it before saving. An incorrect email means the customer will never receive anything. Option A skips the confirmation step. Option C moves on too quickly.

items.customerLine: Yes, all the details are correct.
options: I will update that in our system now.
items.explanation: Option C is the right closing step — the customer has confirmed everything, so you save it and tell them. Option A goes backwards — you already confirmed. Option B repeats a step that is already done.

spotTheMistake.instructions: Read the conversation. Three lines have a mistake. Can you find them?

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Hi. I need to confirm a few details before I set up your account.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Sure. My last name is Wilson.

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Could you say your last name for me? Letter by letter.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: W-I-L-S-O-N. And my email is sam.wilson@company.com.

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Let me read that front to you — sam.wilson@company.com. Is that correct?

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Great. I will refresh that in our system now.

mistakes.explanation: The correct phrase is 'Could you spell that for me?' — not 'say'. 'Spell' means to give each letter one by one. 'Say' just means to speak, which does not help you write the name correctly.
The phrase is 'read that back to you' — not 'front'. 'Reading back' means repeating the information you just received so the customer can check it is correct.
'Update' is the correct word for saving new information in a system. 'Refresh' means reloading a page — it has a completely different meaning and would confuse the customer.
